title: Reliability and Validity of Commercially Available Wearable Devices for Measuring Steps, Energy Expenditure, and Heart Rate: Systematic Review
authors: Fuller D, Colwell E, Low J, Orychock K, Tobin MA, Simango B, Buote R, Van Heerden D, Luan H, Cullen K, Slade L, Taylor NGA
population: 158 publications on nine commercial wearable brands (PubMed, Embase, SPORTDiscus, English language, to May 2019); general and special populations
findings: 158 publications covering nine commercial wearable brands were included; Fitbit was by far the most studied.

In laboratory settings Fitbit, Apple Watch and Samsung appeared to measure steps accurately; heart rate was more variable, with Apple Watch and Garmin the most accurate and Fitbit tending toward underestimation.
For energy expenditure, no brand was accurate.
Overall, devices are accurate for steps and heart rate in laboratory settings, but this varies by manufacturer and device type; devices are upgraded constantly, so more current reviews are needed.
limitations: Mostly laboratory evidence; searches end May 2019 and device generations have changed; no pooled error figures in the abstract; mixes populations and activities and is not running-specific.
implications: Do not use device-reported energy expenditure (kcal) as an input to any load or fuelling calculation.
Treat wrist HR as acceptable under controlled conditions but model quality per device and activity; store device make/model with each activity so an HR-quality flag can be applied.
The chest-strap preference is supported by Navalta 2020 and Gillinov 2017, not by this review.

verification.notes: Crossref confirms title, JMIR mHealth uHealth, 8 Sep 2020, first author Fuller, 12 authors. Abstract read in Europe PMC. Moved the chest-strap implication off this paper since the abstract does not support it.
